events.credibility_reason: Existence and content unverified; known only from an AI-written encyclopedia citation and an unread reference list.

Self-published single-author Zenodo preprint by an author with no visible record in the area; period bounds rest on descent inputs not seen; Lean formalisation covers only core inequalities, sorry status unknown; no expert engagement after one month.
events.ai_basis: The author used large language models throughout the development of this work, including drafting and revising the prose, proposing and developing proof arguments, writing Lean formalizations, and designing and implementing computations.

why: The statement is a yes/no universal claim. Smith's trajectories, the 10^6 check and Neuenschwander's check to 7110200 are finite verifications (instances). Agama and Adje only mention juggler sequences; the OEIS b-file correction concerns step-map values, not termination (none). Prasad is known only by its title, which is about growth constants, a changed question (variant). Agama's date is v4's and the earliest version carrying the remark is unknown, so it is left null. Cochin is the close call. It gives lower bounds on the period of any hypothetical nontrivial cycle, and some of them (at least eight even steps, period at least 22) are unconditional. That moves a quantity on a question that stays open, so it is bound rather than none or case, because it excludes no class of n and does not address divergence. It is unreviewed and doubtful. Its AI disclosure says LLMs were 'proposing and developing proof arguments', which is mathematics in the result. The work is presented as the author's own, so the role is assisted rather than generated.
doubts: Cochin's AI role rests on a generic disclosure with no named model and no account of which arguments came from the LLM; it might arguably be generated. Its scope could also be read as none if the period bounds are judged to be mainly products of finite descent verification.
